Optional lecture B

Calogero–Moser, classical and quantum

What this lecture does

Off the path: nothing on it uses this lecture. Moser’s Lax pair makes a gas in which every pair interacts integrable, with an r\rmatr-matrix that moves with the particles, a kind Lecture 9 only warned about. The reason is that the gas is free motion in disguise: the positions are the eigenvalues of a matrix moving on a straight line. In a harmonic trap every orbit closes after the same time; quantised, the trapped gas has commuting charges with no transfer matrix and an equally spaced spectrum, so every state returns after the same time too.

Present Notes (PDF)

Reading and tutorial. Material marked Reading is studied on your own; material marked Tutorial is worked in the tutorial. Everything else is the lectured core.

B.1 The question

The Toda chain of Lecture 8 and Lecture 9 was integrable with neighbours interacting. Let every pair interact, through g2/(qj−qk)2g^{2}/(q_j-q_k)^{2}g2/(qj​−qk​)2. So the question is

why is a gas in which every particle pushes every other integrable, and why does every trapped orbit, and every trapped quantum state, return after the same time?

The answer: the gas is free motion in a space of matrices, seen through its eigenvalues (Theorems B.8 and B.9); quantum mechanically, the trapped Hamiltonian is conjugate to one that is triangular in the degree (Theorem B.16). The worked example is two particles (Example B.4).

B.2 The model, and Moser’s Lax pair

NNN unit masses on a line, positions q1,…,qNq_1,\dots,q_Nq1​,…,qN​, interacting in pairs: H=12∑j=1Npj2+g2∑j<kV(qj−qk),g>0. H=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_j^{2}+g^{2}\sum_{j<k}V(q_j-q_k),\qquad g>0 . H=21​j=1∑N​pj2​+g2j<k∑​V(qj​−qk​),g>0.(B.1) Four even pair potentials make this integrable (drawn in the first reading):

model V(x)V(x)V(x) motion
rational 1/x21/x^{2}1/x2 scattering
hyperbolic 1/sinh⁡2x1/\sinh^{2}x1/sinh2x scattering, short range
trigonometric 1/sin⁡2x1/\sin^{2}x1/sin2x on a circle, confined
elliptic ℘(x)\wp(x)℘(x) on a circle, confined

℘\wp℘ is Weierstrass’s doubly periodic function (the first reading at the end of this lecture), and the other three are its limits, up to scale and an additive constant, as one or both periods become infinite. The list rational / trigonometric (with hyperbolic) / elliptic is the list of classical r\rmatr-matrices in Lecture 14’s reading; that it recurs is not a coincidence, but this course does not prove it. Every VVV has a double pole at 000 and is repulsive near it, so two particles never meet and keep their (on the circle, cyclic) order. We work with the rational model.

Moser’s Lax matrix fills every off-diagonal slot, one for each pair. With qjk:=qj−qkq_{jk}:=q_j-q_kqjk​:=qj​−qk​ and xxx a real odd function, Ljk=pj δjk+ig x(qjk) (1−δjk),Mjk=−ig x′(qjk) (j≠k),Mjj=−ig∑l≠jV(qjl). L_{jk}=p_j\,\delta_{jk}+\ii g\,x(q_{jk})\,(1-\delta_{jk}),\qquad M_{jk}=-\ii g\,x'(q_{jk})\ (j\ne k),\qquad M_{jj}=-\ii g\sum_{l\ne j}V(q_{jl}) . Ljk​=pj​δjk​+igx(qjk​)(1−δjk​),Mjk​=−igx′(qjk​) (j=k),Mjj​=−igl=j∑​V(qjl​).(B.2) LLL is Hermitian, since xxx is odd, and tr⁡L2=∑jpj2+g2∑j≠kx(qjk)2\tr L^{2}=\sum_jp_j^{2}+g^{2} \sum_{j\ne k}x(q_{jk})^{2}trL2=∑j​pj2​+g2∑j=k​x(qjk​)2, which is 2H2H2H exactly when x2=Vx^{2}=Vx2=V.

Involution is where the model leaves Lecture 9’s method behind.

Proposition B.3 (No numerical r\rmatr). For the rational model with N=2,3N=2,3N=2,3 no constant r\rmatr satisfies {L1,L2}=[r12,L1+L2]\pb{\leg{L}{1}}{\leg{L}{2}}=\comm{\leg{\rmat}{12}}{\leg{L}{1}+\leg{L}{2}}{L1​,L2​}=[r12​,L1​+L2​], nor the weaker two-term form of the reading; for N=3N=3N=3 not even an r\rmatr that depends on the point satisfies the first.

Proof. Each is an inconsistent finite linear system, in exact arithmetic (scripts/check-l11-algebra.py; the points are in the reading). 

What exists is the two-term form with an r\rmatr that depends on the positions cited: Avan and Talon 1993, and the cyclicity argument of Lecture 9’s reading never needed r\rmatr constant, so the FkF_kFk​ are in involution (the reading). The reduction below says why that had to hold.

B.3 Free motion in disguise

Move two 3×33\times33×3 Hermitian matrices along a straight line, X(t)=X0+t P0. X(t)=X_0+t\,P_0 . X(t)=X0​+tP0​.(B.3) Nothing could be freer. Yet the three eigenvalues of X(t)X(t)X(t), straight lines far in the past and future, do not cross: they approach, slow down and turn away, as if they repelled (Figure B.1). For the right X0X_0X0​, P0P_0P0​ they obey exactly the rational Calogero–Moser equations.

Example B.4 (Two eigenvalues and the centrifugal barrier). For N=2N=2N=2 every Hermitian matrix is X=qc1+x⋅σX=q_c\Id+\mathbf x\cdot\boldsymbol\sigmaX=qc​1+x⋅σ, with qc∈Rq_c\in\Rqc​∈R, x∈R3\mathbf x\in\R^{3}x∈R3 and σ\boldsymbol\sigmaσ the Pauli matrices. Its eigenvalues are qc±∣x∣q_c\pm\abs{\mathbf x}qc​±∣x∣, so their gap is s=2∣x∣s=2\abs{\mathbf x}s=2∣x∣. Along (B.3), qcq_cqc​ moves uniformly and x(t)=x0+tv\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf x_0+t\mathbf vx(t)=x0​+tv is a free particle in R3\R^{3}R3. Its distance from the origin feels the centrifugal barrier: with ℓ=x×v\boldsymbol\ell=\mathbf x\times\mathbf vℓ=x×v conserved, ∣v∣2=r˙2+∣ℓ∣2/r2\abs{\mathbf v}^{2}=\dot r^{2}+\abs{\boldsymbol\ell}^{2}/r^{2}∣v∣2=r˙2+∣ℓ∣2/r2, r=∣x∣r=\abs{\mathbf x}r=∣x∣. In terms of the gap, ∣v∣2=14s˙2+4∣ℓ∣2s2,\abs{\mathbf v}^{2}=\tfrac14\dot s^{2}+\frac{4\abs{\boldsymbol\ell}^{2}}{s^{2}},∣v∣2=41​s˙2+s24∣ℓ∣2​, which is the relative energy of two Calogero–Moser particles, 14s˙2+g2/s2\tfrac14\dot s^{2}+g^{2}/s^{2}41​s˙2+g2/s2, with g=2∣ℓ∣g=2\abs{\boldsymbol\ell}g=2∣ℓ∣. The eigenvalues repel because a straight line that misses the origin cannot reach it; they would collide only if ℓ=0\boldsymbol\ell=0ℓ=0.

For NNN particles the rotations become U(N)\U(N)U(N) acting on matrices, the angular momentum becomes [X,P]\comm{X}{P}[X,P], and one idea that N=2N=2N=2 hides is needed: which value to fix it at.

B.4 A conserved commutator, and a level with no collisions

The phase space is Herm(N)×Herm(N)\Herm(N)\times\Herm(N)Herm(N)×Herm(N), points (X,P)(X,P)(X,P) (from here on PPP is a matrix of momenta, not the permutation of Proposition B.3), with the real components of XXX and PPP in an orthonormal basis for tr⁡(AB)\tr(AB)tr(AB) canonical, ω=tr⁡(dX∧dP)\symp=\tr(\dd X\wedge\dd P)ω=tr(dX∧dP), and H=12tr⁡P2H=\tfrac12\tr P^{2}H=21​trP2: a free particle in RN2\R^{N^{2}}RN2. Conjugating both matrices by U∈U(N)U\in\U(N)U∈U(N) is a rotation of RN2\R^{N^{2}}RN2 applied to XXX and to PPP alike, so symplectic, and leaves HHH invariant; the conserved quantity it supplies, by Lecture 2’s Noether principle, is [X,P]\comm{X}{P}[X,P], the momentum map of conjugation (the reading). For N=2N=2N=2 its traceless part is 2iℓ⋅σ2\ii\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma2iℓ⋅σ.

B.5 The reduction: Moser’s LLL is the free momentum

Moser’s LLL is the free momentum PPP in the gauge where XXX is diagonal, so isospectrality is the conservation of PPP; Moser’s MMM is minus the velocity of that gauge. The tr⁡Lk=tr⁡Pk\tr L^{k}=\tr P^{k}trLk=trPk are functions of PPP alone, which Poisson-commute trivially on Herm(N)2\Herm(N)^{2}Herm(N)2, and the Marsden–Weinstein theorem passes brackets of invariant functions to the reduced space: involution is automatic.

B.6 The quantum gas, and its Jastrow ground state

Quantise the trapped rational model, in units ℏ=m=1\hbar=m=1ℏ=m=1 (so the classical Hamiltonian above is the literal classical limit; not the ℏ=2m=1\hbar=2m=1ℏ=2m=1 of Lecture 11’s gas): HC=−12∑j=1N∂j2+∑i<jβ(β−1)(xi−xj)2+ν22∑j=1Nxj2,β≥12. H_{\mathrm C}=-\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{N}\partial_j^{2} +\sum_{i<j}\frac{\beta(\beta-1)}{(x_i-x_j)^{2}} +\frac{\freq^{2}}2\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_j^{2},\qquad \beta\ge\tfrac12 . HC​=−21​j=1∑N​∂j2​+i<j∑​(xi​−xj​)2β(β−1)​+2ν2​j=1∑N​xj2​,β≥21​.(B.8) With ℏ\hbarℏ restored the coupling is ℏ2β(β−1)\hbar^{2}\beta(\beta-1)ℏ2β(β−1), and ℏβ→g\hbar\beta\to gℏβ→g as ℏ→0\hbar\to0ℏ→0. The model is the bosonic Friedrichs extension from functions supported away from every collision, whose eigenfunctions vanish there like ∣xi−xj∣β\abs{x_i-x_j}^{\beta}∣xi​−xj​∣β, the larger of the two possible powers cited: Reed and Simon II, §X.1; the reading says when this is a choice. The function ψ0C=Δβe−ν∑jxj2/2 \psi_0^{\mathrm C}=\Delta^{\beta}e^{-\freq\sum_jx_j^{2}/2} ψ0C​=Δβe−ν∑j​xj2​/2(B.9) satisfies HCψ0C=E0Cψ0CH_{\mathrm C}\psi_0^{\mathrm C}=E_0^{\mathrm C}\psi_0^{\mathrm C}HC​ψ0C​=E0C​ψ0C​ with E0C=ν(N2+βN(N−1)2), E_0^{\mathrm C}=\freq\Bigl(\frac N2+\frac{\beta N(N-1)}2\Bigr), E0C​=ν(2N​+2βN(N−1)​),(B.10) and without the trap HC∣ν=0 Δβ=0H_{\mathrm C}\big|_{\freq=0}\,\Delta^{\beta}=0HC​​ν=0​Δβ=0.

At β=1\beta=1β=1 the state is the Slater determinant of the NNN lowest oscillator states, and (B.10) is ν∑n<N(n+12)\freq\sum_{n<N}(n+\tfrac12)ν∑n<N​(n+21​). It is the ground state of this operator, positive and in its form domain sketched in the reading; positivity alone would not decide it.

B.7 Dunkl operators

Lecture 8 got charges from a Lax matrix, Lecture 14 from a transfer matrix. Here first-order operators commute outright, by carrying a transposition inside them.

Definition B.12 (Dunkl operators). Let sijs_{ij}sij​ exchange the arguments xix_ixi​ and xjx_jxj​ of a function. For i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,Ni=1,…,N put Di=∂i+β∑j≠i1−sijxi−xj. D_i=\partial_i+\beta\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{1-s_{ij}}{x_i-x_j} . Di​=∂i​+βj=i∑​xi​−xj​1−sij​​.(B.11)

DiD_iDi​ maps polynomials to polynomials, (1−sij)f(1-s_{ij})f(1−sij​)f being divisible by xi−xjx_i-x_jxi​−xj​; and sijs_{ij}sij​ is an operator, not a number, so DiD_iDi​ is not a derivation (the tutorial computes the failure of Leibniz’s rule).

At N=2N=2N=2 the commutativity is the translation invariance of x1−x2x_1-x_2x1​−x2​ (the reading); in general:

Theorem B.13 (Commutativity proved in the reading). [Di,Dj]=0\comm{D_i}{D_j}=0[Di​,Dj​]=0 for all i,ji,ji,j, on polynomials.

The first charge is familiar: the deformation cancels pairwise, and ∑iDi=∑i∂i\sum_iD_i=\sum_i\partial_i∑i​Di​=∑i​∂i​ is i\iii times the total momentum. The second is the Hamiltonian. Write Λsym\Lambda^{\mathrm{sym}}Λsym for the symmetric polynomials.

For f∈Λsymf\in\Lambda^{\mathrm{sym}}f∈Λsym, −12∑iDi2f=Δ−β(HC∣ν=0)Δβf=−12∑i∂i2f−β∑i<j∂if−∂jfxi−xj. -\frac12\sum_iD_i^{2}f =\Delta^{-\beta}\Bigl(H_{\mathrm C}\big|_{\freq=0}\Bigr)\Delta^{\beta}f =-\frac12\sum_i\partial_i^{2}f -\beta\sum_{i<j}\frac{\partial_if-\partial_jf}{x_i-x_j} . −21​i∑​Di2​f=Δ−β(HC​​ν=0​)Δβf=−21​i∑​∂i2​f−βi<j∑​xi​−xj​∂i​f−∂j​f​.(B.12) So −12∑iDi2-\tfrac12\sum_iD_i^{2}−21​∑i​Di2​ preserves Λsym\Lambda^{\mathrm{sym}}Λsym and sends its homogeneous component of degree ddd into degree d−2d-2d−2, possibly to zero.

B.8 The trapped spectrum, and isochrony

The whole spectrum follows from Theorem B.14 alone. The homogeneous symmetric polynomials of degree nnn have a basis of monomial symmetric polynomials mκm_\kappamκ​, one for each partition κ\kappaκ of nnn into at most NNN parts.

Theorem B.16 (The trapped spectrum). On Λsym\Lambda^{\mathrm{sym}}Λsym, (ψ0C)−1HC ψ0C=E0C+ν∑ixi∂i−12∑iDi2. \bigl(\psi_0^{\mathrm C}\bigr)^{-1}H_{\mathrm C}\,\psi_0^{\mathrm C} =E_0^{\mathrm C}+\freq\sum_ix_i\partial_i-\frac12\sum_iD_i^{2} . From ∂i2(Gh)=G(∂i2h−2νxi∂ih−νh+ν2xi2h)\partial_i^{2}(Gh)=G(\partial_i^{2}h-2\freq x_i\partial_ih-\freq h +\freq^{2}x_i^{2}h)∂i2​(Gh)=G(∂i2​h−2νxi​∂i​h−νh+ν2xi2​h), G−1(−12∑i∂i2+ν22∑ixi2)(Gh)=−12∑i∂i2h+ν∑ixi∂ih+νN2h,G^{-1}\Bigl(-\frac12\sum_i\partial_i^{2}+\frac{\freq^{2}}2\sum_ix_i^{2}\Bigr) (Gh) =-\frac12\sum_i\partial_i^{2}h+\freq\sum_ix_i\partial_ih+\frac{\freq N}2h ,G−1(−21​i∑​∂i2​+2ν2​i∑​xi2​)(Gh)=−21​i∑​∂i2​h+νi∑​xi​∂i​h+2νN​h, the trap having cancelled. Adding the pair potential and conjugating by Δβ\Delta^{\beta}Δβ, the first term becomes −12∑Di2f-\tfrac12\sum D_i^{2}f−21​∑Di2​f by Theorem B.14, while the Euler operator picks up the degree of Δβ\Delta^{\beta}Δβ: Δ−β∑xi∂i(Δβf)=∑xi∂if+12βN(N−1)f\Delta^{-\beta}\sum x_i\partial_i(\Delta^{\beta}f) =\sum x_i\partial_if+\tfrac12\beta N(N-1)fΔ−β∑xi​∂i​(Δβf)=∑xi​∂i​f+21​βN(N−1)f. The constants assemble into E0CE_0^{\mathrm C}E0C​, which is (B.13).

The right side is triangular in the degree: ∑xi∂i\sum x_i\partial_i∑xi​∂i​ multiplies a homogeneous polynomial of degree ddd by ddd, and −12∑Di2-\tfrac12\sum D_i^{2}−21​∑Di2​ lowers the degree by two or annihilates. On the symmetric polynomials of degree at most ddd the matrix is block-triangular, the block of degree nnn carrying the scalar νn\freq nνn; different blocks carry different scalars, so there is no Jordan obstruction, and the lower-degree part of each eigenvector is solved for recursively. The eigenvalues are νn\freq nνn, n≤dn\le dn≤d, with multiplicity the dimension of the degree-nnn block; let d→∞d\to\inftyd→∞. That these are all the eigenvalues is a density statement: the measure ∣Δ∣2βe−ν∣x∣2dx\abs\Delta^{2\beta}e^{-\freq\abs x^{2}}\dd x∣Δ∣2βe−ν∣x∣2dx has finite exponential moments, so polynomials are dense in its L2L^{2}L2 cited. 

Remark B.17 (The classical face). Classically every trapped orbit returns after 2π/ν2\pi/\freq2π/ν (Corollary B.10), whatever its energy. Quantum mechanically e−iHCte^{-\ii H_{\mathrm C}t}e−iHC​t at t=2π/νt=2\pi/\freqt=2π/ν is a phase times the identity, so every state returns. Neither is a limit of the other: two theorems in the same role, a type-A row of the Dictionary box.

B.9 What it buys

  • A second road to integrability: not an r\rmatr-matrix but a reduction — a free system, a symmetry, a constraint, a gauge fixing (Theorem B.8) — in which Moser’s LLL and MMM are the free momentum and the gauge velocity, and involution is automatic.

  • The motion in closed form (Theorem B.9): momenta permuted and nothing displaced; in a trap, one period for every orbit.

  • A quantum integrable model with no Bethe ansatz and no transfer matrix, whose trapped spectrum is the quantum face of isochrony (Theorem B.16).

B.10 Caveats, in one place

  • Status. Proved here: Theorem B.8(a),(b) and Theorem B.16 (up to the cited density of polynomials). Sketched here, proved in the readings: Theorem B.9, whence Corollary B.10. Proved in the readings: Theorem B.1, Theorem B.2, Theorem B.11, Theorem B.13, Theorem B.14. Cited: the elliptic pair, the dynamical r\rmatr, and the Marsden–Weinstein theorem behind Theorem B.8(c) and the involution by reduction. Proposition B.3 is an exact computation.

  • Only the rational model is reduced here (the others: the readings, cited).

  • The trapped gas: that it has NNN independent classical integrals in involution, and NNN algebraically independent quantum charges, is cited; what is proved is isochrony and the spectrum.

  • No torus on the line: the untrapped gas has no compact level sets, and scatters (the reading).

B.11 Moser’s Lax pair, derived

The Weierstrass function is, for a lattice Λ=2ω1Z+2ω2Z\Lambda=2\omega_1\Z+2\omega_2\ZΛ=2ω1​Z+2ω2​Z in C\CC — here always rectangular, with ω1\omega_1ω1​ real and ω2\omega_2ω2​ purely imaginary, so that ℘\wp℘ is real on the real line with real period 2ω12\omega_12ω1​ — ℘(x)=1x2+∑w∈Λ∖{0}(1(x−w)2−1w2),\wp(x)=\frac1{x^{2}}+\sum_{w\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}} \Big(\frac1{(x-w)^{2}}-\frac1{w^{2}}\Big),℘(x)=x21​+w∈Λ∖{0}∑​((x−w)21​−w21​), even, doubly periodic (℘(x+2ω1)=℘(x+2ω2)=℘(x)\wp(x+2\omega_1)=\wp(x+2\omega_2)=\wp(x)℘(x+2ω1​)=℘(x+2ω2​)=℘(x)), with a double pole at every lattice point. We use nothing else about it. Sending one period to infinity turns it, up to scale and an additive constant, into 1/sin⁡21/\sin^{2}1/sin2 or 1/sinh⁡21/\sinh^{2}1/sinh2; sending both gives 1/x21/x^{2}1/x2 (Perelomov, §3.1). The elliptic model contains the other three as limits. Two of the four potentials, the trigonometric and the elliptic, are periodic, with period d=πd=\pid=π or 2ω12\omega_12ω1​, so the positions matter only modulo ddd: NNN particles on a circle of length ddd, each hemmed in by its neighbours, confined. The cyclic order of the particles is preserved; in each fixed cyclic order a configuration is a point of the circle (where particle 111 is) and NNN positive gaps adding up to ddd (Perelomov, (3.1.16)), so that component of phase space is a circle times an open (N−1)(N-1)(N−1)-simplex, times RN\R^{N}RN for the momenta.

Choosing LLL. Follow Lecture 8’s recipe (§8.4): find LLL with tr⁡L2=2H\tr L^{2}=2HtrL2=2H, then solve for MMM. Every pair interacts, so every off-diagonal slot is used: try

Ljk=pj δjk+ig x(qj−qk) (1−δjk), L_{jk}=p_j\,\delta_{jk}+\ii g\,x(q_j-q_k)\,(1-\delta_{jk}), Ljk​=pj​δjk​+igx(qj​−qk​)(1−δjk​),(B.15) with xxx a real odd function still to be found. Oddness makes LLL Hermitian, since Lkj=ig x(qk−qj)=−ig x(qj−qk)=Ljk‾L_{kj}=\ii g\,x(q_k-q_j)=-\ii g\,x(q_j-q_k)=\overline{L_{jk}}Lkj​=igx(qk​−qj​)=−igx(qj​−qk​)=Ljk​​, and then tr⁡L2=∑jpj2+∑j≠k(ig)2x(qjk) x(qkj)=∑jpj2+g2∑j≠kx(qjk)2,qjk:=qj−qk.\tr L^{2}=\sum_jp_j^{2}+\sum_{j\ne k}(\ii g)^{2}x(q_{jk})\,x(q_{kj}) =\sum_jp_j^{2}+g^{2}\sum_{j\ne k}x(q_{jk})^{2}, \qquad q_{jk}:=q_j-q_k .trL2=j∑​pj2​+j=k∑​(ig)2x(qjk​)x(qkj​)=j∑​pj2​+g2j=k∑​x(qjk​)2,qjk​:=qj​−qk​. Solving for MMM.

The elliptic model. The identity (B.17) with VVV replaced by ℘\wp℘ plus a constant also has odd solutions, built from Jacobi’s elliptic functions, for instance x=cn⁡u/sn⁡ux=\operatorname{cn}u/\operatorname{sn}ux=cnu/snu (Calogero 1975; Perelomov, §3.1, eq. 3.1.12) cited. So all four models have Moser-type Lax pairs without a spectral parameter. Krichever (1980) found the elliptic pair with one, the version that carries a spectral curve (Babelon–Bernard–Talon, §7.4); we do not need it.

B.12 Independence

Proof of Theorem B.2. Expand tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk as a sum over closed walks j1→j2→⋯→jk→j1j_1\to j_2\to\dots\to j_k\to j_1j1​→j2​→⋯→jk​→j1​ through the indices, each step contributing Ljiji+1L_{j_ij_{i+1}}Lji​ji+1​​. A step that stays put contributes a momentum; a step that moves contributes no momentum, and a closed walk that moves at all moves at least twice. So Fk=∑jpjk+RkF_k=\sum_jp_j^{k}+R_kFk​=∑j​pjk​+Rk​ with RkR_kRk​ of degree at most k−2k-2k−2 in the momenta. In the Jacobian det⁡(∂Fk/∂pn)\det(\partial F_k/\partial p_n)det(∂Fk​/∂pn​) the part of top degree in ppp therefore comes from ∑jpjk\sum_jp_j^{k}∑j​pjk​ alone, and it is det⁡(k pnk−1)=N!∏i<j(pj−pi)\det(k\,p_n^{k-1})=N!\prod_{i<j}(p_j-p_i)det(kpnk−1​)=N!∏i<j​(pj​−pi​), the Vandermonde determinant (Lecture 9’s reading). At fixed qqq the Jacobian is a non-zero polynomial in ppp, so, exactly as in Theorem 9.10, the set where it does not vanish is open and dense, and there the dFk\dd F_kdFk​ are independent.

The open Toda chain (Lecture 9’s reading) had independence at every point; here, as for the ring of Lecture 9, a dense open set is what the proof gives, and all that Definition 5.5 asks. With involution (the next reading, or Theorem B.8), the rational Calogero–Moser system satisfies Definition 5.5.

B.13 Involution, and the dynamical r\rmatr-matrix

The linear involution theorem of Lecture 9’s reading, Theorem 9.14, needs a Sklyanin bracket (9.11): a numerical matrix r\rmatr with {L1,L2}=[r,L1+L2]\pb{\leg{L}{1}}{\leg{L}{2}}=\comm{\rmat}{\leg{L}{1}+\leg{L}{2}}{L1​,L2​}=[r,L1​+L2​]. The open Toda chain had one (Proposition 9.21). The same reading also met a weaker, two-term form, which Babelon and Viallet showed always exists behind involution (§9.11): {L1,L2}=[r12,L1]−[r21,L2],r21=Pr12P, \pb{\leg{L}{1}}{\leg{L}{2}} =\comm{\leg{\rmat}{12}}{\leg{L}{1}}-\comm{\leg{\rmat}{21}}{\leg{L}{2}}, \qquad \leg{\rmat}{21}=\perm\leg{\rmat}{12}\perm , {L1​,L2​}=[r12​,L1​]−[r21​,L2​],r21​=Pr12​P,(B.19) with r\rmatr allowed to depend on the point of phase space. When r\rmatr is skew, r21=−r12\leg{\rmat}{21}=-\leg{\rmat}{12}r21​=−r12​, this is (9.11). For Calogero–Moser, a constant r\rmatr does not exist, and for three particles not even a dynamical one in the single-commutator form (Proposition B.3). The computation: for each form and each N=2,3N=2,3N=2,3, the linear equations for a constant r\rmatr are inconsistent at three points at once; for N=3N=3N=3, at the point q=(13,23,53)q=(\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac53)q=(31​,32​,35​), p=(12,−12,−32)p=(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,-\tfrac32)p=(21​,−21​,−23​), g=12g=\tfrac12g=21​, the 818181 linear equations for the entries of a single-commutator r\rmatr are inconsistent, which rules out a dynamical one, since it must work at every point. (For N=2N=2N=2 that system is consistent pointwise, which is why the statement says N=3N=3N=3.) For the N=3N=3N=3 obstruction the mechanism is that of the example in Lecture 9’s reading. At that point, in an eigenbasis of LLL, the matrix L1+L2\leg{L}{1}+\leg{L}{2}L1​+L2​ is diagonal with equal entries in the slots (ij),(ji)(ij),(ji)(ij),(ji), so every commutator with it vanishes there, whatever r\rmatr is; there {L1,L2}\pb{\leg{L}{1}}{\leg{L}{2}}{L1​,L2​} does not. What does exist is the weaker form that the Babelon–Viallet theorem guarantees, with two independent terms, and r\rmatr depending on the positions.

The first sum is skew, P(⋅)P=−(⋅)\perm(\cdot)\perm=-(\cdot)P(⋅)P=−(⋅), and looks like the rational P/λ\perm/\lambdaP/λ of §14.10 with its diagonal removed and the spectral parameter replaced by a position difference. Theorem B.20 (Involution). If LLL satisfies (B.19) for any matrix-valued functions r12\leg{\rmat}{12}r12​, r21\leg{\rmat}{21}r21​ on phase space, then {tr⁡Ln,tr⁡Lm}=0\pb{\tr L^{n}}{\tr L^{m}}=0{trLn,trLm}=0 for all n,mn,mn,m. In particular the Calogero–Moser integrals FkF_kFk​ are in involution.

Proof. Step 1 of Theorem 9.14, the chain rule (9.14), never looked at the bracket. Substituting (B.19), {tr⁡Ln,tr⁡Lm}=nm[tr⁡(A[r12,L1])−tr⁡(A[r21,L2])],A=L1 n−1L2 m−1.\pb{\tr L^{n}}{\tr L^{m}} =nm\Big[\tr\big(A\comm{\leg{\rmat}{12}}{\leg{L}{1}}\big) -\tr\big(A\comm{\leg{\rmat}{21}}{\leg{L}{2}}\big)\Big], \qquad A=\leg{L}{1}^{\,n-1}\leg{L}{2}^{\,m-1}.{trLn,trLm}=nm[tr(A[r12​,L1​])−tr(A[r21​,L2​])],A=L1n−1​L2m−1​. AAA commutes with L1\leg{L}{1}L1​ and with L2\leg{L}{2}L2​ separately (Remark 9.3), and Step 3’s cyclicity argument kills each trace. The values of r\rmatr at the point where the bracket is evaluated are all that enter; that they vary from point to point costs nothing. 

So the machinery did not fail at its first real test. What Lecture 9’s reading proved was more than it assumed: the involution theorem needs only that the bracket is a sum of commutators with L1\leg{L}{1}L1​ and with L2\leg{L}{2}L2​, and Babelon–Viallet (§9.11) says that some such form always exists behind involution. A constant, skew r\rmatr is the exception — the open Toda chain has one — and a dynamical r\rmatr the general situation, as Babelon and Viallet describe it. What does change is Jacobi: Theorem 14.7 (Lecture 14’s reading) was proved for a numerical skew r\rmatr. For their elliptic dynamical r\rmatr, Babelon–Bernard–Talon show by direct calculation a generalised Yang–Baxter equation (7.21), with new terms that are Poisson brackets of LLL with r\rmatr, and that it implies Jacobi cited; in general Jacobi gives a weaker condition, and r\rmatr has gauge freedom. Here Jacobi is not in question: the bracket is the canonical one.

B.14 Scattering, and the comparison with Toda

In the rational model the particles repel and the potential dies away, so, as in §12.4, they separate (Moser). Once they have, L→diag⁡(p)L\to\operatorname{diag}(p)L→diag(p), and the one-line argument after Theorem 12.2 (Lecture 12) applies word for word: the asymptotic momenta are the eigenvalues λ1<⋯<λN\lambda_1<\dots<\lambda_Nλ1​<⋯<λN​ of LLL, arriving in decreasing order along the line and leaving in increasing order (Figure B.5). The scattering is elastic and non-diffractive.

The positions are where Calogero–Moser and Toda part company.

The non-compact fibre again. The hypothesis audit of §9.12 (Lecture 9’s reading) runs as it did for Toda. Involution and independence hold; the flow of F1F_1F1​ translates the whole gas, so no level set is compact; and the flows are complete, by the argument of Proposition 9.23 with one addition: on a level set ∣Ljk∣=g/∣qjk∣\abs{L_{jk}}=g/\abs{q_{jk}}∣Ljk​∣=g/∣qjk​∣ is bounded, so the particles stay a fixed distance apart and the chamber’s walls are never reached (for the Hamiltonian flow itself, Theorem B.9(a) says so directly). The torus conclusion fails, and what replaces it is scattering. (One line of generalisation: Ruijsenaars and Schneider (1986) found a relativistic deformation of these models, still integrable, the elliptic case included (Ruijsenaars 1987); a reading below.)

B.17 Conjugation, its momentum map, and the reduction theorem

The core used a handful of facts about conjugation without proof. Here they are, with the general theorem behind the reduction.

Lecture 5’s proof (§5.5) used an action of Rn\R^{n}Rn, its orbits and its stabilisers (Definition 5.8). The same words, for any group:

Definition B.23 (Group action, orbit, stabiliser). An action of a group GGG on a set S\mathcal SS assigns to each U∈GU\in GU∈G a map ΦU:S→S\Phi_U:\mathcal S\to\mathcal SΦU​:S→S with Φ1=id⁡\Phi_{\Id}=\idΦ1​=id and ΦU∘ΦV=ΦUV\Phi_U\circ\Phi_V=\Phi_{UV}ΦU​∘ΦV​=ΦUV​. The orbit of s∈Ss\in\mathcal Ss∈S is {ΦU(s):U∈G}\{\Phi_U(s):U\in G\}{ΦU​(s):U∈G}; its stabiliser is Gs={U:ΦU(s)=s}G_s=\{U:\Phi_U(s)=s\}Gs​={U:ΦU​(s)=s}, a subgroup.

Orbits partition S\mathcal SS. Points on one orbit have conjugate stabilisers, GΦV(s)=VGsV−1G_{\Phi_V(s)}=VG_sV^{-1}GΦV​(s)​=VGs​V−1; for the abelian group of Lemma 5.9 that made them equal.

Herm(N)\Herm(N)Herm(N), the N×NN\times NN×N Hermitian matrices, is a real vector space of dimension N2N^{2}N2 (NNN real diagonal entries, N(N−1)/2N(N-1)/2N(N−1)/2 complex ones above the diagonal), and ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(AB) \inner{A}{B}=\tr(AB) ⟨A,B⟩=tr(AB)(B.23) is a Euclidean inner product on it: tr⁡(A2)=∑j,k∣Ajk∣2\tr(A^{2})=\sum_{j,k}\abs{A_{jk}}^{2}tr(A2)=∑j,k​∣Ajk​∣2. The differences qj−qkq_j-q_kqj​−qk​ are not an accident of notation. (Olshanetsky and Perelomov’s generalisation, below, keeps every model of Figure B.2 integrable; this is where slN\sllie_NslN​ comes from.) The constraint of Theorem B.8 is one equation per root space, and the Calogero–Moser potential is a sum over the positive roots α\alphaα of g2/α(q)2g^{2}/\alpha(q)^{2}g2/α(q)2. For N=3N=3N=3, in the plane q1+q2+q3=0q_1+q_2+q_3=0q1​+q2​+q3​=0 where the centre of mass has been removed, the three positive roots are drawn in Figure B.11: each is a pair of particles, and its hyperplane α(q)=0\alpha(q)=0α(q)=0 is where that pair would collide. Olshanetsky and Perelomov (1976) replaced AN−1A_{N-1}AN−1​ by other root systems RRR: H=12∣p∣2+∑α∈R+gα2 V(α(q)),H=\tfrac12\abs{p}^{2}+\sum_{\alpha\in R_+}g_\alpha^{2}\,V\big(\alpha(q)\big),H=21​∣p∣2+α∈R+​∑​gα2​V(α(q)), with couplings gαg_\alphagα​ equal on roots related by the Weyl group. For BCNBC_NBCN​ (which contains BNB_NBN​, CNC_NCN​, DND_NDN​ as special couplings) and VVV rational, hyperbolic or trigonometric, they constructed a Lax pair, and so proved Liouville integrability, for couplings obeying one further relation: with ggg on the roots ej±eke_j\pm e_kej​±ek​, g1g_1g1​ on eje_jej​ and g2g_2g2​ on 2ej2e_j2ej​, either g1=0g_1=0g1​=0 or g12+2 g1g2−2g2=0g_1^{2}+\sqrt2\,g_1g_2-2g^{2}=0g12​+2​g1​g2​−2g2=0 (Perelomov, §3.9, Proposition 2) cited. The exceptional systems are integrable too, but Perelomov records no Lax pair for them. For BNB_NBN​, CNC_NCN​, DND_NDN​ the positive roots include ej+eke_j+e_kej​+ek​ as well as ej−eke_j-e_kej​−ek​ (and eje_jej​ or 2ej2e_j2ej​), so particle jjj interacts also with the mirror image of particle kkk and, for BNB_NBN​ and CNC_NCN​, with a wall at the origin. For those couplings they obtained the rational and hyperbolic models by projecting free motion on symmetric spaces of zero and negative curvature, and the trigonometric one from positive curvature — the construction of this lecture, with Herm(N)\Herm(N)Herm(N) one example (Perelomov, §3.3). In the same spirit, Kazhdan, Kostant and Sternberg obtained the trigonometric model 1/sin⁡21/\sin^{2}1/sin2 by replacing the matrix XXX with a unitary matrix, so that its eigenvalues live on a circle cited. Root systems return in optional lecture C, as the Dynkin diagrams indexing nested Bethe equations.

B.20 Ruijsenaars–Schneider

Ruijsenaars and Schneider (1986) found a one-parameter deformation of every Calogero–Moser model, still integrable, that behaves like a relativistic particle system: with ccc a “speed of light” and unit masses, the rational one is HRS=c2∑j=1Ncosh⁡pjc∏k≠j(1+g2c2(qj−qk)2)1/2=Nc2+HCM+O(c−2)H_{\mathrm{RS}}=c^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\cosh\frac{p_j}{c} \prod_{k\ne j}\Big(1+\frac{g^{2}}{c^{2}(q_j-q_k)^{2}}\Big)^{1/2} =Nc^{2}+H_{\mathrm{CM}}+O(c^{-2})HRS​=c2j=1∑N​coshcpj​​k=j∏​(1+c2(qj​−qk​)2g2​)1/2=Nc2+HCM​+O(c−2) (Arutyunov, (1.67); the expansion is checked in scripts/check-l12-algebra.py). It too comes from reduction: the rational model from the cotangent bundle of the group GL(N)\GL(N)GL(N) in place of the matrix space (Arutyunov, §2.2.1), and the hyperbolic one from a Poisson–Lie deformation of that, the “Heisenberg double” (§2.2.2) cited. This course does not develop either. The elliptic case is Ruijsenaars (1987). Its quantum version is beyond this course.

Near a collision the relative coordinate r=xi−xjr=x_i-x_jr=xi​−xj​ sees −∂r2+β(β−1)/r2-\partial_r^{2}+\beta(\beta-1)/r^{2}−∂r2​+β(β−1)/r2, whose solutions behave as rpr^{p}rp with p(p−1)=β(β−1)p(p-1)=\beta(\beta-1)p(p−1)=β(β−1): two exponents, p=βandp=1−β, p=\beta\quad\text{and}\quad p=1-\beta , p=βandp=1−β,(B.27) which the coupling does not distinguish checked. Fix β≥12\beta\ge\tfrac12β≥21​, choosing the larger — a labelling convention, not a stability condition, since β(β−1)=(β−12)2−14\beta(\beta-1)=(\beta-\tfrac12)^{2}-\tfrac14β(β−1)=(β−21​)2−41​ never falls below the Hardy bound −14-\tfrac14−41​, which it attains at β=12\beta=\tfrac12β=21​, where the exponents coincide and the second solution is r1/2ln⁡rr^{1/2}\ln rr1/2lnr.

Definition B.30 (The model, completely). Take the ordered chamber — x1<⋯<xNx_1<\dots<x_Nx1​<⋯<xN​ on the line, and 0≤x1<⋯<xN<π0\le x_1<\dots<x_N<\pi0≤x1​<⋯<xN​<π on the circle, where xN−x1→πx_N-x_1\to\pixN​−x1​→π counts as a collision too — and define the operator as the Friedrichs extension of (B.8) or (B.25) from the smooth functions compactly supported away from every collision. On this domain an eigenfunction behaves at a collision as ψ=O(∣xi−xj∣β),xi→xj, \psi=O\bigl(\abs{x_i-x_j}^{\beta}\bigr),\qquad x_i\to x_j , ψ=O(∣xi​−xj​∣β),xi​→xj​,(B.28) the larger of the two exponents in (B.27). For β≥32\beta\ge\tfrac32β≥23​ the Friedrichs extension is the only self-adjoint one, the other branch r1−βr^{1-\beta}r1−β being not even locally square-integrable; for 12≤β<32\tfrac12\le\beta<\tfrac3221​≤β<23​ the operator is not essentially self-adjoint, and (B.28) is what picks this extension out of the family cited: Reed and Simon II, §X.1 and its appendix. For (B.25) there is a second, global condition: the model is bosonic and periodic, so a state extends from the chamber to a symmetric function of period π\piπ in each coordinate.

Two conventions follow and are used throughout. Restricting to the chamber and extending bosonically to RN\R^{N}RN are unitarily equivalent up to N!\sqrt{N!}N!​, so a symmetric function on RN\R^{N}RN and a function on the chamber are the same object; and Δ=∏i<j(xj−xi)\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)Δ=∏i<j​(xj​−xi​) is positive there, so the symmetric function Δβ\Delta^{\beta}Δβ names is ∣Δ∣β\abs\Delta^{\beta}∣Δ∣β. And (B.28) describes eigenfunctions, not the whole operator domain, which contains functions with no pure power behaviour at all.

Why it is the ground state, and why positivity is not the reason

The usual argument is that a positive eigenfunction of a Schrödinger operator on a connected domain is the ground state. That is true, and here it needs a hypothesis that is easy to drop.

Remark B.31 (The partner exponent). Replacing β\betaβ by 1−β1-\beta1−β in ψ0S\psi_0^{\mathrm S}ψ0S​ changes neither (B.25) nor the positivity of the function on the chamber, and Theorem B.11’s computation — which used only the exponent — makes it solve the same differential equation with the value (1−β)2N(N2−1)/6(1-\beta)^{2}N(N^{2}-1)/6(1−β)2N(N2−1)/6, strictly smaller than E0SE_0^{\mathrm S}E0S​ for β>12\beta>\tfrac12β>21​ checked. So positivity alone cannot identify the ground state. What excludes the partner is Definition B.30, and the test is sharper than it looks: at N=2N=2N=2 the partner leaves L2L^{2}L2 exactly at β=32\beta=\tfrac32β=23​, but for N≥3N\ge3N≥3 the binding collision is the total one, where Δ1−β\Delta^{1-\beta}Δ1−β is homogeneous of degree (1−β)N(N−1)/2(1-\beta)N(N-1)/2(1−β)N(N−1)/2 in N−1N-1N−1 relative coordinates and its square is integrable only for β<1+1/N\beta<1+1/Nβ<1+1/N. A cluster of mmm particles gives β<1+1/m\beta<1+1/mβ<1+1/m, and 1+1/m1+1/m1+1/m decreases in mmm, so the total collision is the sharpest of the N−1N-1N−1 tests. At N=3N=3N=3, β=75\beta=\tfrac75β=57​ every pair test passes and the triple collision diverges checked. So the honest statement is that (B.9) is positive, lies in the form domain of Definition B.30, and is the ground state of that operator sketched.

B.25 Dyson’s three ensembles

Remark B.36 (The ground state is a random-matrix ensemble). In the variable (B.31), ∣ψ0S∣2∝∏i<j∣zi−zj∣2β\abs{\psi_0^{\mathrm S}}^{2}\propto\prod_{i<j}\abs{z_i-z_j}^{2\beta}​ψ0S​​2∝∏i<j​∣zi​−zj​∣2β on the unit circle, which up to normalisation is the joint eigenvalue density of Dyson’s circular ensemble of index 2β2\beta2β cited: Dyson (1962); Mehta ch. 11. The repulsion exponent is the Jastrow exponent: P(s)∼s2βP(s)\sim s^{2\beta}P(s)∼s2β as s→0s\to0s→0 is the vanishing of ψ0S\psi_0^{\mathrm S}ψ0S​ at a collision, squared.

B.26 What is shared with the Bethe ansatz, and what is not

Nothing in this lecture was an RRR-matrix: no auxiliary space, no monodromy matrix, no RTTRTTRTT relation, and Corollary B.15 is not { dkln⁡t(λ) }\{\,\dd^{k}\ln t(\lambda)\,\}{dklnt(λ)} for any ttt — the tower of Lecture 15’s reading comes from one transfer matrix and one solution of the Yang–Baxter equation, while IkI_kIk​ comes from NNN operators that commute before anything is traced. Nor was there a Bethe ansatz: Proposition B.35 reports the answer in Bethe form rather than obtaining it. Both are claims about the route; the trigonometric model does carry a braid-group structure, Cherednik’s, and the next reading says where.

What is shared: infinitely many commuting charges, one of them the Hamiltonian; a many-body problem fixed by two-body data, one exponent β\betaβ per pair, with free particles at shifted momenta; and non-diffractive scattering (Lecture 12, Lecture 13) in the strongest form there is, the phase shift being constant. The difference is where the structure sits: in Lecture 14 and Lecture 15 in an algebra of operators on an auxiliary space, here in the symmetric group.

B.27 Creation operators, Cherednik’s operators, and exclusion statistics

Four continuations, each of which is a small subject.

What the charges are, and what they are not. IkI_kIk​ of Corollary B.15 is a differential–difference operator of order kkk involving every particle; it is not a sum of local densities of bounded range, and there is no lattice here for Definition 19.1 to apply to. The family is also not the one Theorem B.1 produced classically: tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk quantises to something with ordering ambiguities, and the Dunkl construction sidesteps that question rather than answering it. What is true is that the IkI_kIk​ commute, that I2I_2I2​ is the Hamiltonian, and that NNN of them are algebraically independent — which is the count Liouville would have asked for cited: Polychronakos (1992).

Cherednik’s operators. The DiD_iDi​ of (B.11) are the rational Dunkl operators, and Theorem B.33 did not use them: the Sutherland model needed its own conjugation, done by hand. There is a trigonometric analogue, Cherednik’s: commuting first-order differential–difference operators in zzz, built from zj∂zjz_j\partial_{z_j}zj​∂zj​​ and the transpositions, whose algebra is the degenerate affine Hecke algebra — and that is where the braid relations hidden in this model live. Two distinctions are easy to lose. Fractional exclusion statistics. The density equation after Proposition B.35 reads ρt=12π−(β−1)ρ\rho_t=\tfrac1{2\pi}-(\beta-1)\rhoρt​=2π1​−(β−1)ρ: each root present removes β−1\beta-1β−1 vacancies beyond the one it occupies. Haldane read this as a statistics interpolating between bosons and fermions, with β=1\beta=1β=1 the fermionic point where nothing is removed. The thermodynamics is then a one-line modification of Lecture 17’s counting — the binomial coefficient (LρtdλLρdλ)\binom{L\rho_t\dd\lambda}{L\rho\dd\lambda}(LρdλLρt​dλ​) of Proposition 17.4 acquires a β\betaβ-dependent number of slots — and reproduces the Calogero–Sutherland free energy cited: Haldane (1991); Wu (1994). B.28 The frontier, and reduction as a construction principle

Four directions lead out of this course. Classification. Which R(λ)\Rmat(\bethe)R(λ) solve the Yang–Baxter equation? Classically there is a theorem: Belavin and Drinfeld sorted the non-degenerate solutions of (14.12) for a simple Lie algebra into rational, trigonometric and elliptic families. Quantum mechanically no list is closed, even for a two-dimensional auxiliary space and even of difference form, and the Hubbard model’s R\RmatR (optional lecture C) is of no difference form at all. The systematic language is quantum groups: Yangians and affine quantum algebras, whose representations are the R\RmatR-matrices. Separation of variables. Sklyanin’s method replaces the Bethe ansatz by a change of variables to the eigenvalues of B(λ)B(\bethe)B(λ) — and on the homogeneous chain BBB lowers SzS^{z}Sz by one, so it is nilpotent and there are none to change to, and the construction must twist the monodromy first. (The pseudovacuum was never the problem: Lecture 15 built it.) It is where the spectral curve det⁡(z−T(λ))\det(z-\mono(\bethe))det(z−T(λ)) of Lecture 9’s reading returns, as a quantum spectral curve. Beyond Euler. Equation (20.5) is the leading order; diffusive corrections, and the anomalous transport of the isotropic Heisenberg chain, are current work. Integrable circuits. Discrete-time quantum circuits built from solutions of Yang–Baxter are integrable models in which everything here can be recomputed, and are the form in which the subject has reached quantum simulators.

And one principle. This lecture built the Calogero–Moser system out of free motion on Herm(N)\Herm(N)Herm(N), a symmetry, a moment-map constraint and a gauge fixing. Reduction returns in three places, all of them beyond this course.

Quantum Hamiltonian reduction. The classical recipe has an operator version: free motion becomes the Laplacian on a group, the constraint becomes a representation-theoretic condition, and the radial part of the Laplacian is the Calogero–Sutherland operator of §B.21. This is why the Dunkl operators of §B.7 look like covariant derivatives: they are.

Nested systems from root systems. The Calogero–Moser models are indexed by root systems (§B.19), and so are the nested Bethe equations of optional lecture C, by the Cartan matrix of the same diagram.

Spectral curves. The curve of §9.13 (Lecture 9’s reading) is a reduction too, of a much larger linear problem, and the modern statement — that integrable systems of this type are classified by moduli of curves with data on them — is the subject that reading’s pointer was aiming at.

What all three share is the shape of Theorem B.8: a free system, a symmetry, a constraint and a choice of gauge. It is worth carrying out of the course as a question to ask of any solvable model — what is it a reduction of?

The Bohr–Sommerfeld rule of Lecture 6’s reading is therefore exact here in the sense semiclassics always means it, and this is the cheapest place in the course to see what the Langer correction is for.

(e) Sutherland at N=2N=2N=2. On the circle, ψ0S=sin⁡βr\psi_0^{\mathrm S}=\sin^{\beta}rψ0S​=sinβr and E0S=β2⋅2⋅3/6=β2E_0^{\mathrm S}=\beta^{2}\cdot2\cdot3/6=\beta^{2}E0S​=β2⋅2⋅3/6=β2; and (B.32) gives k1,2=2κ1,2±βk_{1,2}=2\kappa_{1,2}\pm\betak1,2​=2κ1,2​±β, so Eκ=12[(2κ1+β)2+(2κ2−β)2]E_\kappa=\tfrac12\bigl[(2\kappa_1+\beta)^{2}+(2\kappa_2-\beta)^{2}\bigr]Eκ​=21​[(2κ1​+β)2+(2κ2​−β)2]. At β=1\beta=1β=1, κ=0\kappa=0κ=0, that is E=1E=1E=1 with momenta ±1\pm1±1: the two impenetrable bosons of Girardeau’s map (Lecture 18’s reading), which are one antiperiodic fermion pair. The formal value β=0\beta=0β=0 gives free bosons at rest, E=0E=0E=0 — the one exponent at which the shift disappears, and the only one at which the ground state is not an ensemble. It lies outside Definition B.30’s β≥12\beta\ge\tfrac12β≥21​, being the partner of β=1\beta=1β=1.

Summary

  • The model (B.1) and Moser’s pair (B.2) (Theorem B.1); no numerical r\rmatr (Proposition B.3).
  • Free motion in disguise: on the level [X,P]=ig(eeT−1)\comm{X}{P}=\ii g(ee^{T}-\Id)[X,P]=ig(eeT−1) the eigenvalues never collide, and fixing XXX diagonal turns PPP into Moser’s LLL (Theorem B.8).
  • The positions are the eigenvalues of Q(0)+tL(0)Q(0)+tL(0)Q(0)+tL(0) (Theorem B.9); trapped, every orbit closes at 2π/ν2\pi/\freq2π/ν (Corollary B.10).
  • Quantum: Dunkl charges with no transfer matrix (Corollary B.15); the trapped spectrum E0+νnE_0+\freq nE0​+νn (Theorem B.16): every state returns at 2π/ν2\pi/\freq2π/ν.
